Title: This Week in Democracy: Iran War Whiplash, Voter Purges, and Rising Calls to Rein in Trump
Content:
The week opened with a symbolic and substantive shift in how the United States describes its own power. Over the weekend, the administration formally renamed the Department of Defense the Department of War, a rebranding that matched President Trump’s increasingly aggressive posture toward Iran. Aides reportedly urged him to treat Iranian civilian infrastructure as a legitimate military target, and he used public appearances and social media to threaten action over the Strait of Hormuz. When pressed about the laws of war, he brushed aside questions about war crimes and suggested that bombing civilian infrastructure would not violate international law. At the same time, he berated NATO allies for failing to help reopen the strait, calling them cowardly and again threatening to pull the United States out of the alliance. The combination of a new “War” label on the Pentagon, open talk of striking civilian targets, and threats to unravel NATO signaled a week in which traditional restraints on the use of force would be tested.

Even before the shooting stopped, the economic consequences of the Iran confrontation began to show up in everyday life. Over the weekend, Amazon announced a 3.5 percent surcharge on third‑party sellers, and the U.S. Postal Service imposed an 8 percent fuel surcharge, both citing higher logistics costs tied to the conflict and disruptions around Hormuz. These were early indicators of a broader inflationary shock that would crest by Friday, as oil prices rose and supply chains adjusted to a chokepoint under pressure. The link between foreign policy decisions and domestic prices, often abstract, became concrete in shipping fees and postage.

On the same weekend, immigration enforcement illustrated how national security rhetoric can bleed into domestic targeting. Federal agents revoked green cards and detained two women described by Senator Marco Rubio as relatives of slain Iranian commander Qassem Soleimani, despite disputed family ties, placing them in Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody for deportation. In another case, a nearly blind Rohingya refugee was reportedly abandoned by border agents in a Buffalo parking lot and later died; the death was ruled a homicide. These incidents unfolded alongside a federal judge’s finding that border agents in California had violated a prior order by conducting warrantless arrests. Taken together, they showed immigration tools being used against people linked—accurately or not—to foreign adversaries, and vulnerable refugees being treated in ways that courts increasingly describe as unlawful.

While federal power concentrated, civil society began organizing its own response. Indivisible co‑founder Ezra Levin announced plans for a nationwide May Day general strike on May 1 under the slogan “No Work, No School, No Shopping,” with unions and advocacy groups starting to coordinate logistics and strike funds. The proposed action, framed as a protest against authoritarian trends, aimed to use economic disruption as a form of civic pressure. At the border, Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem invoked statutory waiver powers to set aside environmental and historic protections in order to push a steel bollard wall through Big Bend National Park and adjacent Texas parkland, despite local opposition. The move underscored how executive discretion can override longstanding safeguards for public lands in the name of security.

By Monday, the focus shifted from war abroad to control over who can participate in elections at home. Trump signed an executive order directing the Department of Homeland Security to use the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) immigration database to compile a list of “confirmed U.S. citizens” eligible to vote. He ordered the Department of Justice to prosecute anyone who distributed ballots to people not on that list. SAVE was built to check eligibility for public benefits, not to define the electorate, and is known to misidentify citizens as non‑citizens. The order effectively pressured states to rely on an error‑prone federal tool for voter purges, shifting practical control over the franchise toward the executive branch and raising the risk that eligible citizens would be swept off the rolls.

Congress, meanwhile, struggled to assert its constitutional role over war and presidential fitness. House Republicans shut down a pro forma session to prevent Democrats from forcing a vote to limit Trump’s war powers over Iran, continuing a pattern from earlier in March when both chambers narrowly rejected measures requiring congressional approval for Iran operations. As Trump’s rhetoric grew more extreme, Senator Chris Murphy publicly raised the possibility of invoking the 25th Amendment, and Representative Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on House Judiciary, formally requested a cognitive exam for the president, citing his recent statements and posts. Yet procedural maneuvers kept Congress from debating either war powers or capacity in a sustained way, leaving high‑risk decisions concentrated in the executive.

The administration also moved to reshape public health policy along ideological lines. Under Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the department implemented deep cuts to routine childhood immunizations and state public‑health funding, and officials spread misinformation during a measles outbreak. HHS proposed ending Medicare and Medicaid payments to hospitals providing gender‑affirming care to minors, directly targeting access to care for transgender youth. In contrast, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention quietly renewed the charter of its immunization advisory committee, a small sign of continuity in evidence‑based practice amid politicization. Courts provided some counterweight elsewhere: a California judge ruled that border agents had violated a prior order by conducting warrantless arrests in Sacramento, a Massachusetts judge blocked the termination of Temporary Protected Status for more than 5,000 Ethiopians, and historians and transparency advocates sued over an Office of Legal Counsel opinion declaring the Presidential Records Act unconstitutional, warning that the administration planned to stop complying with preservation rules.

Press freedom came under direct pressure as well. At a Monday press conference, Trump again threatened to jail journalists who refused to reveal the source of a leak about a missing U.S. airman in Iran, invoking national security. The threat echoed a similar one reported the previous day and fit into a broader pattern of hostility toward leaks and investigative reporting. At the same time, Trump extended his influence into state politics by endorsing former Fox host Steve Hilton in the California governor’s race, promising federal help, while Wisconsin voters elected liberal Chris Taylor to their state supreme court, expanding a 5–2 liberal majority. That Wisconsin result, in a key swing state, is expected to shape rulings on redistricting, abortion, unions, and election disputes—an example of state‑level institutions adjusting the balance of power even as the federal executive centralizes it. Online, an artificial‑intelligence‑generated image purporting to show a smiling U.S. airman rescued in Iran went viral on X, illustrating how synthetic media can distort public understanding of wartime events.

On Tuesday, the Iran crisis reached a new level of volatility. Trump posted that “a whole civilization will die tonight” if Iran did not meet his demands, suggesting possible use of tactical nuclear weapons and threatening annihilation of Iranian civilization. Under the Geneva Conventions and customary international law, deliberate attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure are prohibited, but Trump’s rhetoric treated such constraints as optional. Iran had already closed or restricted the Strait of Hormuz in response to Israeli strikes and U.S. pressure, driving up global oil prices. Later that day, after talks involving Pakistani leaders, Trump abruptly announced he would suspend bombing Iran for two weeks, claiming the United States had met its objectives and was close to a peace deal based on a 10‑point Iranian proposal widely seen as favorable to Tehran. The swing from nuclear‑tinged threats to a short ceasefire, without congressional authorization or clear terms, underscored how decisions about war and peace were being made in a highly personalized, improvisational way.

Even as the bombs paused, the war drove a boom in speculative defense projects. The administration allocated at least $17.5 billion more to the Golden Dome space‑based missile defense system, on top of $25 billion the prior year, as part of a $1.5 trillion defense budget. Much of this spending would move through budget reconciliation, a process that allows certain budget measures to pass with a simple majority and limited debate, curbing oversight. SpaceX and Palantir—companies tied to major Trump donors Elon Musk and Peter Thiel—were expected to receive multi‑billion‑dollar contracts for satellites and software. Analysts questioned whether the system could work on the promised timeline, noting it might not be operational until at least 2035. Congress remained on recess, and Republican leaders showed no intention of recalling members despite the escalating crisis, leaving earlier narrow votes against binding war‑powers limits as the last word.

Courts and advocates continued to document and challenge immigration abuses. A Massachusetts judge postponed the effective date of ending Temporary Protected Status for Ethiopians, finding likely violations of administrative law and pretext in the government’s rationale. Another court expanded relief to require daily clergy access at an Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facility. In New York, Latino residents filed a class action alleging that the Department of Homeland Security, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and Customs and Border Protection had a policy of stopping and arresting people based solely on perceived Latino ethnicity. A report on the Dilley family detention center described inhumane conditions and lasting harm, which the Department of Homeland Security denied. Separately, the Department of Justice’s civil rights division opened an investigation into former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson for allegedly lying to Congress about Trump’s role in the January 6 insurrection, an unusual assignment for that division and one that raised concerns about using enforcement tools against a key witness. Outside the courtroom, the Electronic Frontier Foundation’s analysis of 12 million searches in Flock’s license‑plate reader network showed law enforcement using the system to search around major protests, even as at least 53 cities across 20 states moved to cancel, reject, or sharply limit Flock contracts after community campaigns and revelations of unauthorized federal access.

By Wednesday, the ceasefire Trump had announced was already unraveling. Israel signaled it had not agreed to halt bombardment of southern Lebanon and continued attacks, while Iran retaliated against Saudi and Kuwaiti energy and water infrastructure and further restricted access to the Strait of Hormuz. Tehran required ships to obtain permission and pay cryptocurrency tolls, tightening its grip on a key maritime chokepoint. Oil prices climbed, and confusion grew over Trump’s claim of a joint U.S.–Iran toll venture, which Iranian officials publicly mocked. The breakdown of a hastily announced ceasefire, with no clear multilateral framework and no congressional role, showed how ad‑hoc diplomacy can fail, leaving global markets and security exposed.

The week also revealed how emerging technologies are being folded into wartime decision‑making under conditions of cronyism. Reporting showed that the Pentagon, now under the “War” label and led on technology by Emil Michael, had entered an artificial‑intelligence agreement with Elon Musk’s xAI as part of a broader push to deploy advanced AI across the department. Michael held a financial interest in xAI until shortly after the deal, raising conflict‑of‑interest concerns. On the same day, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit denied Anthropic’s emergency motion to stay a competing AI contract but granted expedited review, citing the government’s need to secure AI technology during active conflict. The combination of insider ties and judicial deference to wartime discretion highlighted how ethics and accountability can be sidelined when procurement is framed as urgent national security.

In Congress, a different kind of accountability fight played out over the Jeffrey Epstein files. The Department of Justice announced that former Attorney General Pam Bondi would not appear for a subpoenaed deposition about the handling of Epstein records, arguing she had been subpoenaed only in her official capacity. The House Oversight Committee insisted the subpoena was personal and warned of contempt. Ranking member Robert Garcia backed First Lady Melania Trump’s call for a public hearing with survivors, but survivors criticized her statement as shifting burdens onto them while the Justice Department had not fully complied with the Epstein Transparency Act. The dispute showed how high‑profile abuse cases can become arenas for narrative control, with survivor access to information and justice caught between institutional defensiveness and political positioning. Elsewhere, the Environmental Protection Agency’s administrator, Lee Zeldin, delivered a keynote at a Heartland Institute conference, attacking mainstream climate science and praising repeal of the “endangerment finding” that underpins U.S. climate regulations, moving climate denial from the fringe to the helm of environmental policy.

Wednesday also brought more evidence of how protest and dissent are policed. The Electronic Frontier Foundation’s analysis of Flock license‑plate reader data confirmed that law enforcement had searched for vehicles around major protests, while a separate report detailed how a Department of Homeland Security agent’s projectile blinded a student at the No Kings march in Los Angeles despite an injunction limiting force. Dozens of cities moved to cancel or restrict Flock contracts over privacy and federal‑access concerns, reflecting local efforts to set boundaries on surveillance tools that can chill assembly. In the information sphere, Trump escalated attacks on media narratives about Iran, labeling a CNN report suggesting Iran had achieved a significant victory as “fraud” and demanding a retraction. He lashed out at former allies who criticized his Iran policy, calling them “stupid people” and not true supporters. Branding unfavorable coverage as fraudulent and ostracizing dissenters within his own camp further narrowed the space for independent assessment of war outcomes.

On Thursday, the constitutional struggle over war powers and presidential fitness sharpened. House Democrats attempted to pass a resolution to curtail Trump’s Iran war powers using unanimous consent, but the Republican pro forma speaker refused to recognize them and ended the session. This followed earlier Republican moves to block war‑powers votes. Meanwhile, more than 85 House Democrats and two senators publicly called for invoking the 25th Amendment or impeachment after Trump’s threats to annihilate Iranian civilization. House Democratic leadership scheduled a virtual briefing on the issue, and Raskin’s request for a cognitive exam remained unanswered. Procedural control allowed a minority to shield expansive war‑making from debate even as a large bloc of lawmakers questioned the president’s capacity, deepening a constitutional standoff.

The same day, financial regulators took steps that favored politically connected markets. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission filed unprecedented lawsuits against Arizona, Connecticut, and Illinois to stop them from regulating political prediction markets run by platforms such as Kalshi, Polymarket, Crypto.com, and Robinhood, arguing that federal jurisdiction preempted state efforts. Many of these firms have business ties to Trump and have donated to his political operations. Separately, the administration quietly ended a Securities and Exchange Commission investigation into Crypto.com that had begun under President Biden, taking no enforcement action despite the company’s close ties to Trump Media. These moves suggested a regulatory environment in which federal agencies not only declined to police politically connected firms but actively sued states that tried, raising questions about impartiality and the monetization of politics.

Immigration stories continued to accumulate, forming a pattern rather than isolated abuses. A detailed report from Raíces and Human Rights First documented due‑process violations and degrading conditions at the Dilley detention center, including contaminated food and inadequate medical care. In a separate case, the Board of Immigration Appeals issued a final removal order for activist Mahmoud Khalil, who alleges political retaliation. A Canadian mother and her seven‑year‑old daughter described nearly three weeks in unsafe Immigration and Customs Enforcement facilities before release on bond with ankle monitoring. Meanwhile, the Eswatini Supreme Court ruled that four men deported from the United States have the right to meet with a local lawyer after months without in‑person counsel, an instance of a foreign court stepping in to protect rights where U.S. processes had failed. In Florida, Governor Ron DeSantis signed anti‑Sharia legislation, aligning with a “Sharia Free Caucus” that portrays Muslim immigration as an invasion aimed at imposing religious law. Writing suspicion of Muslims into statute normalized policy built on religious animus rather than concrete legal problems.

Civil society, for its part, continued to mobilize. The May Day Strong coalition held a national organizing call to coordinate May 1 actions under the theme “Workers Over Billionaires,” sharing toolkits and a map of local events. Separately, the LGBTQ advocacy group Glisten organized its 30th annual Day of Silence, encouraging students and adults to take a vow of silence to highlight anti‑LGBTQ harassment and legislative attacks in schools. These actions, alongside local moves to limit surveillance, showed communities using both economic disruption and symbolic protest to defend workers’ rights and LGBTQ students amid hostile policy environments. Transparency advocates also turned to the courts: the Democracy Forward Foundation sued the Department of Justice for failing to respond to Freedom of Information Act requests about communications and agreements related to voter registration data and election integrity efforts, while the National Health Law Program sued Health and Human Services and the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services for withholding records on data‑sharing with Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement involving Medicaid enrollees. These suits aimed to uncover how sensitive data might be used in ways that affect who can safely vote or access health care.

Thursday ended with another example of how presidential rhetoric can reshape expectations of accountability. The Wall Street Journal reported that Trump told staff he would issue mass pardons for anyone who had been near the Oval Office, a statement the White House later called a joke. That evening he posted a graphic video depicting violence and attacking Haitian immigrants and Joe Biden, shortly after Melania Trump’s Epstein‑related press conference. Promising blanket pardons for insiders and circulating violent, dehumanizing content from the presidency both weakened deterrence for misconduct and normalized extreme rhetoric in political discourse.

By Friday, the economic and humanitarian costs of the Iran conflict were fully visible. With Iran tightening control over the Strait of Hormuz and charging fees for passage, oil prices rose above $100 per barrel. U.S. inflation reached 3.3 percent, the highest since 2024, with gas up 21 percent, fuel oil 31 percent, and airfares 15 percent in March alone. The University of Michigan Consumer Sentiment Index fell to a record low of 47.6, worse than during the 2008 financial crisis or the pandemic. These numbers captured how foreign policy choices and chokepoint politics were feeding directly into higher living costs and deep public pessimism about the economy. At the same time, The New York Times verified that U.S.–Israeli strikes had damaged at least 22 schools and 17 health facilities in Iran, while Iran’s Red Crescent reported even higher numbers. Under the laws of armed conflict, schools and hospitals are protected civilian objects unless used for military purposes; independent confirmation of damage to these sites underscored the humanitarian toll and strengthened calls to scrutinize potential violations of international law.

Domestically, the administration moved to centralize control over another key public resource: forests. Officials announced a sweeping restructuring of the U.S. Forest Service, closing all regional offices, consolidating 57 research facilities into one site, moving headquarters to Salt Lake City, and replacing regional offices with 15 politically appointed state directors. The federal employees’ union called the move illegal under budget restrictions and warned it would degrade public‑land management. Replacing career regional leadership with political appointees and shuttering research sites weakened professional stewardship of public lands and opened the door to partisan control over forests and fire policy. Courts and regulators, however, continued to provide partial checks in other areas. A Texas court overturned the death sentence of Clarence Curtis Jordan, a man with intellectual disabilities who had been on death row for nearly 50 years, citing constitutional standards. In Washington, a judge ordered the Pentagon to comply with an earlier ruling protecting press access and struck down a rebranded leak‑solicitation policy, rejecting an attempt to evade judicial oversight. The Federal Communications Commission finalized rules requiring licensees to disclose foreign adversary control of communications networks, and the Environmental Protection Agency published multiple Environmental Impact Statements for public comment, modest reminders that some regulatory processes still functioned in regular order.

The week closed with further signs that the presidency was being used to advance personal projects and foreign alignments. Reports revealed that Trump had used foreign steel to construct a $400 million White House ballroom, undercutting his “America First” rhetoric. On social media he pledged to use U.S. economic resources to support Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán in an upcoming election, signaling support for an illiberal foreign leader. He reiterated promises of mass pardons for staff and continued to post violent, anti‑immigrant content. These actions, combined with regulatory favors for Trump‑linked firms and the reorientation of agencies like the Forest Service and Environmental Protection Agency, pointed to a governing style increasingly oriented around personal and factional interests rather than institutional norms.

Across the week, democratic life was shaped by the interplay of concentrated executive power, partial institutional resistance, and civic mobilization. The Iran conflict showed how quickly decisions about war, made with minimal congressional input and loose regard for civilian protections, can reverberate through global markets and domestic prices. Moves to define voter eligibility through a federal immigration database, to hide or reinterpret records laws, and to tilt financial regulation toward allies all raised questions about who controls the rules of participation and accountability. Courts, state elections, local governments, and civil‑society groups did not reverse these trends, but they did mark out lines of resistance—from blocking some immigration abuses and protecting press access to organizing strikes and student actions. The week’s record is one of institutions under strain, with the balance between unilateral power and shared governance actively contested rather than settled.

Title: This Week in Democracy: War Powers Tested, Pardons Promised, and Accountability Contested
Content:
The week unfolded under the shadow of two intertwined struggles: over war and over the rule of law. Abroad, the president escalated and then abruptly tried to contain a confrontation with Iran, testing the limits of unilateral war‑making. At home, he leaned on clemency and a compliant Justice Department to ease consequences for allies and January 6 leaders, even as courts, Congress, and civil society tried to reassert basic constraints.

Over the weekend, the White House made clear how it now understood presidential mercy. Donald Trump commuted former congressman George Santos’s seven‑year fraud sentence after only three months and publicly highlighted his earlier pardon of Binance founder Changpeng Zhao. Reporting indicated he was privately promising mass end‑of‑term pardons for anyone who had worked near the Oval Office. The press secretary described the pardon power as “absolute,” signaling that clemency was being treated less as a tool for correcting injustice and more as a shield for insiders and favored economic actors. That same pattern would reappear later in the week as the Justice Department moved to undo hard‑won convictions from the January 6 attack.

At the same time, Trump escalated sharply against Iran. Over the weekend he warned that “a whole civilization will die tonight” if Iran defied him, language widely read as genocidal. He then announced a U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports and the Strait of Hormuz, claiming other countries would join even as NATO allies declined. He later boasted that U.S. forces had “completely obliterated” the Iranian navy, saying 158 ships were destroyed, and threatened to sink any remaining vessels approaching the blockade. Undertaken without new congressional authorization, these moves put enormous pressure on global shipping and energy markets and set the stage for a week of improvised diplomacy and contested war powers.

Domestically, the weekend also brought signs of politicized justice in the immigration system. The Justice Department abruptly fired six immigration judges, including two Biden appointees who had recently blocked deportations of pro‑Palestinian students from Tufts and Columbia and who had higher‑than‑average asylum grant rates. The dismissals, coming alongside surveillance footage that undercut ICE agents’ accounts in a Minneapolis shooting case and led to dropped charges, raised alarms that immigration adjudication was being reshaped to favor enforcement outcomes over legal independence.

States continued to pull power upward from local communities. In Missouri, Republicans mandated that Kansas City devote a quarter of its budget to policing and returned St. Louis’s police to state control, limiting local authority over public safety. In North Carolina, the state supreme court declined to enforce the long‑standing Leandro school‑funding precedent despite years of underfunding, while lawmakers steered millions to crisis pregnancy centers and expanded private‑school vouchers. Educators began organizing rallies and advocacy days in response, seeing public education funding and local control as central to democratic self‑government.

Congress, meanwhile, showed both its capacity and its limits. Over the weekend the House passed a bill, 224–204, to allow roughly 350,000 Haitians to retain Temporary Protected Status for three years after DHS terminated it, with a handful of Republicans joining Democrats. The vote directly defied the administration’s deportation agenda and asserted legislative authority over immigration status, even as the bill faced an uncertain future in the Senate and a looming Supreme Court case on TPS terminations.

Civil society activity threaded through these institutional battles. The We Are America March set off on a 160‑mile trek from Philadelphia to Washington to build sustained, visible opposition to authoritarianism. Bruce Springsteen opened a Los Angeles concert with a call to defend democracy and the Constitution. Indivisible prepared a national day of action against ICE warehouse detention, while Bernie Sanders and New York City councilmember Zohran Mamdani launched the Union Now initiative to boost union density and support strikes. Abroad, large protests in Hungary targeted Viktor Orbán’s authoritarian rule. These efforts, alongside housing reform advocacy and a decision by AI firm Anthropic to delay public release of a powerful model over security concerns, showed citizens and private actors trying to shape the conditions of daily life where formal politics seemed constrained.

By Monday, institutional pushback became more visible. The California Supreme Court formally disbarred John Eastman for deceptive work in efforts to overturn the 2020 election, ordering him off the roll of attorneys and imposing financial penalties. In Washington, a federal judge, acting on an appellate remand, narrowed an injunction against Trump’s plan for a 90,000‑square‑foot White House ballroom, allowing only underground construction deemed necessary for security and blocking the above‑ground addition. Together, these rulings signaled that courts were still willing to enforce professional and legal limits on attempts to subvert elections and on efforts to reframe personal projects as national security needs.

At the same time, the administration moved to weaken economic oversight and expand unilateral trade power. It sought to end the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau’s headquarters lease years early and asked a court to approve cutting its staff to about one‑third of prior levels, sharply reducing federal capacity to police consumer‑finance abuses. After a Supreme Court ruling against parts of his tariff regime, Trump claimed authority to reimpose tariffs under a different statute, Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, testing how far a president can go in reshaping trade without Congress. These moves built on earlier legislation that had cut corporate taxes and oversight, shifting power toward large firms and the executive branch.

Transparency advocates turned to the courts as agencies stalled. Environmental and watchdog groups sued EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin for failing to issue required fine‑particle pollution designations, sued the Office of Management and Budget over FOIA delays, and filed cases seeking records on the “Gold Card” visa program. Other suits targeted the Election Assistance Commission for FOIA delays tied to election integrity. These cases underscored how, when agencies ignore statutory duties, FOIA and environmental litigation become central tools for enforcing transparency and environmental protections.

Economic strain was increasingly visible. Labor Department data showed inflation rising to 3.3 percent, with wholesale inflation at 4 percent, the highest in three years, driven in part by war‑related energy prices. The White House staged a photo opportunity with a DoorDash driver dubbed “DoorDash Grandma” to promote a “no tax on tips” policy allowing up to $25,000 in tips to be deducted from taxable income. Critics noted that the event highlighted deeper failures in health care, labor rights, and retirement security, as the worker relied on gig work to support her family. The symbolism of a narrow tax tweak for tipped workers contrasted with the broader impact of earlier laws that had cut Medicaid and corporate taxes, and with the inflationary pressures tied to trade wars and Middle East conflict.

On Tuesday, concerns about presidential fitness moved from commentary into legislative form. In response to Trump’s extreme rhetoric about Iran and his self‑depiction as Jesus, House Democrats led by Jamie Raskin introduced legislation to create a standing commission to assess presidential capacity under the 25th Amendment. A related proposal with 50 Democratic co‑sponsors sought a formal mechanism to evaluate a president’s ability to discharge the duties of office. Raskin also requested a comprehensive neuropsychological assessment from Trump’s physician. In a House controlled by the president’s allies, these measures were unlikely to advance, but they marked an attempt to operationalize constitutional tools for addressing questions about presidential stability and judgment.

The Justice Department’s approach to January 6 shifted further. DOJ lawyers asked an appeals court to dismiss seditious‑conspiracy convictions of Proud Boys and Oath Keepers members and moved in district court to vacate similar convictions, invoking the “interests of justice.” At the same time, prosecutors filed new terrorism‑related charges against the suspect accused of planting pipe bombs near party headquarters on January 6. The contrast suggested a narrowing of accountability for organized insurrectionists closely tied to Trump, even as other strands of January 6 violence continued to be prosecuted.

Elsewhere on Tuesday, the D.C. Circuit granted a writ of mandamus to halt a district court’s criminal‑contempt inquiry into officials who had defied a deportation temporary restraining order, citing separation‑of‑powers concerns. New litigation challenged a mid‑decade partisan gerrymander, and Democracy Forward sued the Election Assistance Commission over FOIA delays. Additional suits targeted agencies over the treatment of pregnant youth in federal custody and environmental decisions. These cases illustrated how courts can both shield executive deliberations and serve as venues to contest gerrymanders, secrecy, and rights violations.

Economic and health‑care pressures deepened. Reporting revisited Trump’s 2025 law cutting roughly $900 billion from Medicaid over a decade, affecting nearly 12 million people, and highlighted state decisions to end or restrict Medicaid coverage for GLP‑1 weight‑loss drugs. A Farm Bureau survey found that 70 percent of U.S. farmers could not afford enough fertilizer due to soaring costs, which analysts tied to trade disruptions and conflict. Producer price inflation reached 4 percent, reinforcing the link between earlier fiscal choices—deep health‑care cuts and corporate tax breaks—and current foreign policy in driving up costs and reducing care for low‑income people and farmers.

Questions of secrecy and elite accountability surfaced in another arena when Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche announced that DOJ would stop releasing documents related to Jeffrey Epstein, despite a congressional subpoena and ongoing public interest. House Democrats moved toward holding former Attorney General Pam Bondi in contempt for failing to appear before the Oversight Committee about the files and pressed for a new deposition. The decision to halt releases in such a high‑profile case raised concerns about selective secrecy and the enforceability of congressional subpoenas.

By Wednesday, the Iran confrontation took a sudden turn. After days of threats and a naval blockade, Trump announced a ceasefire and proposed a framework under which the U.S. and Iran would jointly manage the Strait of Hormuz. In Congress, Senator Bernie Sanders and allies pushed resolutions to block bomb and bulldozer sales to Israel, while House and Senate leaders scheduled war powers votes aimed at requiring Trump to seek authorization for further military action in Iran and other countries. Sanders’s resolutions ultimately failed but drew support from 40 Democrats, signaling a shift away from unconditional military aid. War powers resolutions in both chambers sought to limit Trump’s authority to continue Operation Epic Fury, reflecting growing unease with open‑ended conflicts driven by presidential discretion.

Domestic oversight of security and health policy intensified. Testimony revealed that budget director Russell Vought had slashed global health funding, including the PEPFAR program, and inconsistently released appropriated funds, prompting a Government Accountability Office finding of impoundment violations. Vought defended a $1.5 trillion defense budget request and denied illegal fund withholding. In a separate House hearing, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. faced questions about a Trump‑Vance initiative on health‑care fraud and alleged pardons for fraudsters tied to campaign contributions, highlighting how budget and pardon decisions can redirect resources from public health to defense and potentially reward politically connected offenders.

Civil society marked Tax Day with organizing and protest. The ACLU’s California arm held a rapid‑response training to prepare participants to respond to threats against rights and institutions. Across the country, Tax Day protests highlighted oligarchy, billionaire influence, war spending, and the gap between public needs and political priorities. Democracy Docket published an opinion urging close tracking of litigation that shapes election rules and democratic access. These actions showed citizens building skills and narratives to contest concentrated wealth and defend voting rights outside formal party structures.

In a notable public intervention from the judiciary, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson used a speech at Yale Law School to criticize the Supreme Court’s conservative majority for repeatedly using unexplained emergency orders to allow controversial Trump policies to take effect despite lower‑court findings that they were likely illegal. She argued that this “shadow docket” practice undermines transparency and affects real people without full briefing or opinions. Her remarks underscored how opaque Supreme Court procedures can quietly reshape policy and weaken checks on executive power.

Thursday brought the sharpest test of congressional war powers. A resolution by Democrat Greg Meeks to block further military action against Iran under the War Powers Act failed in the House by a single vote, 213–214. Republican Thomas Massie broke with his party to support it, while Democrat Jared Golden opposed it. A related resolution to block Operation Epic Fury also failed by one vote. The razor‑thin margin showed how close Congress came to reasserting its constitutional role and how a handful of members can determine whether large‑scale military operations proceed without explicit authorization.

On the same day, the Justice Department announced it would move to vacate seditious‑conspiracy convictions of Oath Keepers and Proud Boys leaders involved in January 6, following Trump’s earlier commutations of their sentences. Prosecutors again invoked the “interests of justice.” Combined with the president’s prior clemency for 14 leading members of these groups, the move effectively unwound much of the accountability for organized insurrection. It also tied back to the weekend’s talk of mass pardons, reinforcing a through‑line in which loyalty to the president could outweigh the legal consequences of attacking the transfer of power.

House Democrats responded to the administration’s military posture by filing six articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The articles accused him of unauthorized military action against Iran, deadly strikes on suspected drug‑smuggling boats, mishandling classified information, concealing civilian casualties, and punishing a senator for reminding service members of their rights. In a Republican‑controlled House, the effort was unlikely to succeed, but it marked a formal attempt to hold a senior security official accountable for uses of force and retaliation against oversight.

Oversight of public health policy also sharpened. RFK Jr. testified before House committees, defending his decision to end CDC pro‑vaccine messaging and facing criticism for promoting misinformation and controversial comments about Black children. Lawmakers questioned his proposed cuts to medical research and his use of HHS resources, including a video with musician Kid Rock. A separate hearing probed his role in the health‑care fraud initiative and alleged pardons for politically connected fraudsters. The hearings highlighted how public health can be reshaped by misinformation and political favoritism, with direct consequences for vaccine uptake and trust.

Beyond Washington, higher education and civil rights came under strain. Hampshire College in Massachusetts announced it would permanently close after the upcoming fall semester due to low enrollment and financial pressure, advising faculty and staff to seek unemployment. At the same time, the Coalition for Action in Higher Education organized a National Day of Action to defend accessible, politically independent universities, building on prior campus teach‑ins and protests. In the political arena, some Republicans, including Representative Andy Ogles and House Speaker Mike Johnson, escalated Islamophobic rhetoric, with Ogles saying Muslims “don’t belong in American society” and Johnson warning about Sharia law. The comments, aimed at mobilizing parts of the base, stigmatized a religious minority and deepened social divisions.

The week’s Iran arc looped back to economic leverage. Despite the U.S. naval blockade, Iran shipped nine million barrels of crude from floating storage in the Gulf of Oman, challenging the blockade’s effectiveness. Simultaneously, the U.S. and Iran negotiated the release of up to $20 billion in frozen Iranian funds for humanitarian purposes, up from an earlier $6 billion offer, as part of efforts to end the war and address Iran’s enriched uranium stockpile. The developments underscored both the limits of unilateral sanctions and blockades and the centrality of financial tools in war‑ending diplomacy.

Money and access intersected in domestic politics as well. Reporting revealed a confidential email from Sinan Kanatsiz, a figure in Trump’s political network, soliciting $500,000 contributions to Turning Point USA’s PAC in exchange for a “one‑on‑one meeting and private photo with President Donald Trump.” Kanatsiz confirmed the solicitation, calling it a “big request,” and said no one had yet accepted. The offer, if taken up, would formalize a pay‑to‑play dynamic in which six‑figure donations buy personal access to the president, deepening the role of money in political influence.

On Friday, attention turned to the independence of key institutions and the long tail of earlier policy choices. Trump threatened to remove Federal Reserve chair Jerome Powell, whose term was nearing its end, while Powell was under criminal investigation over alleged cost overruns on Fed building renovations. Powell has said he will remain on the board until the investigation concludes. The threat fit a pattern of presidential efforts to influence monetary policy and personnel at the central bank, blurring the line between legitimate oversight and political retaliation.

Congress, still divided over surveillance and civil liberties, approved a 10‑day extension of FISA Section 702, the warrantless surveillance authority used to collect foreign intelligence, just days before its scheduled sunset. Internal Republican divisions and opposition from a coalition of progressive Democrats and hardline Republicans demanding reforms—such as warrants for Americans’ communications—blocked a longer renewal. The stopgap preserved broad surveillance powers while postponing decisions on stronger privacy safeguards, keeping civil liberties and national security in unresolved tension.

Environmental protections suffered a significant setback when the Senate voted 50–49 to repeal a 20‑year ban on mining near Minnesota’s Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness, following earlier House approval. The resolution, expected to be signed by Trump, cleared the way for Twin Metals Minnesota, a subsidiary of Chilean mining giant Antofagasta, to pursue copper‑sulfide mining upstream of the wilderness. Environmental groups warned of serious pollution risks to a major protected area and to local economies built around a pristine landscape, illustrating how short‑term extraction and foreign corporate interests were being prioritized over long‑term environmental safeguards.

Oversight efforts continued on other fronts. House Democrats opened an investigation into Jared Kushner’s Middle East dealings, focusing on potential conflicts of interest between his business ventures and U.S. policy. Oversight Democrats also pressed for a new deposition of Pam Bondi over the Epstein files after she skipped a subpoenaed appearance, as the committee moved toward holding her in contempt. These probes tested whether Congress could meaningfully investigate conflicts of interest and potential cover‑ups involving powerful insiders.

Civil society closed the week with a visible win and continued organizing. After employees and customers protested Philz Coffee’s decision to remove Pride flags—gathering more than 7,300 petition signatures and engaging with San Francisco Pride leaders—the company reversed course, reinstated the flags, and issued an apology. The episode showed how coordinated employee and customer pressure can defend visible support for marginalized groups. Meanwhile, the National Day of Action for higher education proceeded, and Tax Day and labor initiatives continued to build momentum, keeping democratic engagement alive in workplaces and on campuses.

Beneath the headline fights, regulators quietly advanced a raft of environmental, health, and safety rules. EPA issued notices on Environmental Impact Statements and approved air‑quality plan revisions in Virginia, decisions that will shape local pollution levels. OSHA assumed safety authority at certain Department of Energy sites and revoked an obsolete marine‑terminal standard, affecting workplace protections. The FDA announced public meetings and rule changes on animal drugs, vaccines, and research oversight, influencing drug access and safety. The National Archives invited public comment on proposed records schedules from multiple agencies, giving the public a say in what government records are preserved or destroyed and, by extension, what future generations will be able to know about this period.

Taken together, the week showed U.S. democracy straining under concentrated executive power in war‑making, clemency, and economic policy, even as other institutions tried to respond. Congress came within a single vote of reclaiming war powers and used hearings and investigations to probe pardons, public health, and conflicts of interest. Courts disbarred a key election lawyer, constrained a presidential construction project, and heard challenges to secrecy and environmental inaction, while a Supreme Court justice warned about the Court’s own opaque practices. At the same time, civil society—through marches, campus actions, union organizing, and local campaigns—worked to defend public education, vulnerable communities, and basic norms of inclusion. The balance between these forces, and the records they leave behind, will shape how this era is judged and what tools remain for those who come after.

Title: This Week in Democracy: Immigration Powers Expand, Oversight Fights Back, and Pressure on the Press Deepens
Content:
The week opened with three storylines already in motion, but one quickly emerged as the strongest: immigration enforcement was no longer just a matter of raids and rhetoric. It was expanding through budgets, personnel decisions, court rulings, and new theories about who could be removed and under what conditions. Alongside that, the war with Iran drove a separate but connected struggle over money, oversight, and protest, while a clash involving FBI Director Kash Patel widened from a defamation dispute into a test of how far federal power could be used against journalism. By week’s end, those threads had spread across Congress, the courts, federal agencies, and the states.

Over the weekend, the administration asked Congress for $200 billion for the war with Iran, immediately turning foreign policy into a domestic fight over spending and accountability. Questions surfaced about whether traders had profited from well-timed bets tied to the conflict, and by Sunday the administration’s own public messaging on the war and on negotiations was already showing strain. Contradictory statements and visible confusion did more than create political embarrassment. They sharpened a deeper question that would run through the week: who was making decisions, who stood to benefit, and what tools remained for public oversight once a war footing had been established.

At the same time, pressure on the press began to take a more formal shape. Kash Patel first threatened and then filed a $250 million defamation suit against *The Atlantic* over reporting on his conduct. Because Patel was not a private citizen but the sitting FBI director, the case immediately carried implications beyond reputational combat. A senior law-enforcement official was using civil litigation against a major news outlet, a move that risked chilling scrutiny not only of him but of the office he held. What began as a legal dispute would not stay confined to the courthouse.

The weekend also offered an early view of how immigration and voting rules were converging. New reporting showed that ICE had deported 174 DACA recipients in 2025, a sign that even people long treated as partially shielded from removal were vulnerable in practice. In North Carolina, lawmakers advanced a bill allowing voter citizenship challenges and broader sharing of voter data with federal authorities. House Democrats, meanwhile, tried to build an answer on a different front, launching a task force on ethics and self-dealing and introducing legislation aimed at preventing presidents and vice presidents from misusing taxpayer funds. And inside the Justice Department, a profile of Harmeet Dhillon’s Civil Rights Division described a broad shift away from traditional anti-discrimination enforcement and toward claims of anti-white bias, with investigations increasingly announced through social media as public spectacle as much as legal action.

By Monday, the war story had moved decisively into Congress. Senate Democrats prepared subpoenas tied to possible financial conflicts around the Iran war, and Representative Jamie Raskin opened an inquiry into Jared Kushner’s overlap between diplomacy and Saudi-backed business interests. The conflict’s political economy was becoming a central issue. The question was no longer only whether the war was justified or sustainable, but whether wartime decision-making had become entangled with private gain, influence networks, and opaque diplomacy. In a system where Congress has limited leverage once military action is underway, oversight of money and conflicts of interest became one of the few available checks.

Public dissent was visible the same day, but so were its limits. More than 70 veterans and military family members were arrested while protesting the Iran war inside the Cannon House Office Building. Their arrests came just after a failed war-powers effort and as administration officials acknowledged that Trump’s own public commentary had complicated diplomacy with Iran. The juxtaposition was stark: visible antiwar resistance in the Capitol, but little sign that Congress could translate that resistance into binding restraint. The war was producing protest, yet formal institutional brakes remained weak.

Immigration, meanwhile, widened from a weekend warning into a full governing project. The House’s earlier extension of Temporary Protected Status for Haitians remained alive, but the administration’s direction was clearer elsewhere. ICE detained the wife of an Army sergeant despite prior protection, Senate Republicans prepared a large reconciliation package for ICE and Border Patrol, and new litigation and community-rights trainings showed both the spread of enforcement and the effort to help people navigate it. Monday also brought a familiar display of presidential power used in different registers at once: symbolic clemency for January 6 participants remained a marker of how Trump rewarded political allies, while new memorandums invoked defense-readiness logic to expand domestic fossil-fuel production. Across policy areas, the presidency was being used to move faster, reward friends, and bypass slower regulatory channels.

The Patel story also deepened on Monday. His lawsuit against *The Atlantic* was filed and refiled across the news cycle, while Attorney General Pam Bondi refused to appear for a congressional subpoena and new Freedom of Information Act litigation added to the day’s fights over access to information. The pattern was becoming clearer. The same officials facing scrutiny were also shaping the legal and informational conditions under which that scrutiny would proceed. Accountability was no longer just about what had happened, but about whether records, testimony, and reporting could still reach the public.

Tuesday brought a more structural turn in immigration policy. The administration had fired six more immigration judges over the weekend, including judges who had blocked some deportations, and border-wall construction in Big Bend moved forward despite local opposition. Congress and advocacy groups were also fighting over voter-registration data and immigration protections, showing how immigration policy was spilling into elections and federal-state relations. These were not isolated personnel or construction decisions. They pointed to an effort to reshape the institutions that decide who can stay, who can vote, and what information governments can demand in the process.

That same day, surveillance and voter-data fights moved to the center. Congress passed a 10-day extension of Section 702 after broader renewal efforts faltered, preserving warrantless surveillance authority while reform efforts remained unresolved. Common Cause sued the Justice Department over demands for unredacted statewide voter rolls, and American Oversight sued multiple agencies over Palantir-related records. The connection between these disputes was not accidental. All turned on the same democratic tension: the government’s appetite for data was broadening, while the public’s ability to learn how that data was being used remained contested and often dependent on litigation.

Tuesday also showed how institutional weakening can happen quietly. The administration ended the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau headquarters lease early and sought to shrink the agency dramatically, while tariff refunds opened for importers rather than consumers. None of this had the drama of abolishing an agency outright, but it fit a familiar pattern. Public-facing regulatory capacity was being reduced through staffing, leases, and procedure, leaving private actors better positioned to absorb the benefits. In the information sphere, platforms removed AI-generated pro-MAGA influencer accounts, a TikTok network spread AI-generated Iranian military propaganda, and Trump dismissed new negative polling as rigged. Shared facts were under pressure from synthetic media, partisan rhetoric, and the weakening of institutions meant to mediate public trust.

Wednesday turned the Patel matter into something larger and more serious. Reports revealed that the FBI had investigated *New York Times* reporter Elizabeth Williamson after she wrote about Patel’s use of government resources. That disclosure landed alongside a new congressional inquiry into Patel’s conduct and security-clearance disclosures. The story had now crossed a line. What began as a defamation suit by a powerful official against a news outlet had become a broader question about whether federal investigative power was being used to shield that official from scrutiny. For journalism, the issue was no longer merely hostility from officeholders. It was the possibility of state retaliation.

The same day, culture-war and civil-rights conflicts moved through states, schools, and Congress. Florida barred local governments from funding diversity, equity, and inclusion programs and from pursuing climate-related initiatives. An Iowa court upheld restrictions tied to LGBTQ topics and book removals. A new report found that book bans reached a record high in 2025, and the House Oversight Committee targeted LGBTQ-related content in a North Carolina school district. These were not disconnected local skirmishes. They showed coordinated pressure on what schools, libraries, and local governments could teach, fund, or even acknowledge. In North Carolina and Virginia, election and information fights intensified as Republicans moved to share voter data with the administration, the Republican National Committee sued over voter ID procedures, and a court blocked voter-approved congressional maps. Representation, voter access, and control over election data were all under active contest before any ballots were cast.

Protest remained part of the week’s story as well. The earlier arrests of antiwar veterans stayed in focus, and in Colorado a federal immigration agent was charged after allegedly assaulting a protester during a demonstration over detained asylum seekers. That combination mattered. It suggested both the vulnerability of protest to force and the continuing, if uneven, possibility of accountability when officials crossed legal lines.

Thursday was the week’s heaviest day, and immigration dominated it. Senate Republicans approved a budget resolution for $140 billion in immigration enforcement funding, using reconciliation to move around the filibuster. At the same time, the administration’s enforcement apparatus was visibly expanding through federal deployments, reassigned agents, and a larger ICE footprint. What had begun as pressure was becoming system-building. The administration was not only enforcing existing law more aggressively; it was financing and institutionalizing a larger machinery for doing so.

Then came a further escalation: reports said the administration was pushing the Justice Department to pursue denaturalization cases against 384 people. That moved beyond the deportation of noncitizens and into the status of naturalized citizens themselves. Denaturalization has always carried special weight because it changes the meaning of citizenship. If legal belonging can be reopened and revoked, citizenship becomes less secure and more conditional, especially for people whose status was once thought settled. By Thursday, the week’s immigration story had widened from border enforcement to the legal foundations of membership in the polity.

The war story also hardened on Thursday. A Democratic bill to end the Iran war was blocked, underscoring Congress’s inability to impose a legislative check on the conflict. Trump then reposted a call to kill Iranians who opposed a deal, adding inflammatory rhetoric to a week already marked by war spending, antiwar arrests, and diplomatic strain. The combination of weak legislative restraint and escalating presidential language made the conflict feel both less accountable and more volatile.

Thursday also opened a new front in the struggle over records and secrecy. The Freedom of the Press Foundation and Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington sued over an Office of Legal Counsel opinion declaring the Presidential Records Act unconstitutional and over White House recordkeeping practices that could endanger preservation of presidential records. The same day brought court wins for NPR and PBS and a protest-permit lawsuit against the National Park Service. Together, these cases showed how much of the week’s accountability fight had shifted into court. The issue was not only whether current officials could be checked, but whether the records needed for future oversight would survive at all.

Another Thursday dispute, smaller in scale but revealing in structure, centered on the Scotts Valley casino fight. A federal court said the Interior Department had violated the Scotts Valley Band’s due-process rights, while reporting tied a $2 million donation to Trump’s super PAC to efforts by a rival tribe to influence the same regulatory dispute. The case connected campaign money, lobbying, tribal sovereignty, and federal administrative power in unusually direct fashion. It was a reminder that regulatory decisions can become vehicles for political influence even in areas where sovereign tribal interests are at stake. Meanwhile, the Justice Department’s indictment of the Southern Poverty Law Center remained a major civil-society concern, with critics increasingly viewing it alongside pressure on journalists and protest groups as part of a broader willingness to use legal process against watchdogs and ideological opponents.

Friday closed the week by confirming where the immigration story had been heading. The Board of Immigration Appeals ruled that DACA status alone does not require termination of removal proceedings, potentially making it easier for the government to continue deportation cases against hundreds of thousands of recipients. Coming after reports of DACA deportations, the firing of immigration judges, the new enforcement funding, and denaturalization plans, the ruling narrowed one of the procedural buffers that had helped protect Dreamers from full exposure to the deportation system. It did not stand alone; it capped a week in which immigration enforcement had expanded across budgets, personnel, legal doctrine, and the meaning of citizenship itself.

Friday also brought a stark assertion of punitive state power. The Justice Department announced that it would expand federal execution methods to include firing squads, electrocution, and gas asphyxiation, while reviving a harder federal death-penalty posture overall. In a week defined by the widening reach of coercive institutions, this was one of the clearest statements of governing philosophy: the state was broadening, not narrowing, the tools through which it could punish.

The week ended with more conflict over information. The CDC blocked publication of a report showing COVID-19 vaccine effectiveness, adding scientific suppression to a week already full of fights over records, surveillance, and disclosure. Litigation over presidential records continued, and court-ordered disclosures in other cases underscored how much public accountability now depended on judges forcing information into the open. Secondary stories remained in motion as well: Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders approved a merger with Paramount Skydance amid continuing scrutiny of media concentration, and the Justice Department dropped its probe into Jerome Powell, easing one pressure point on an independent economic institution.

Taken together, the week showed expansion and counterpressure rather than a single decisive break. Immigration enforcement advanced through money, staffing, legal rulings, and new threats to settled status. The Iran war continued to shape domestic politics through spending requests, protest, market questions, and oversight demands that Congress struggled to convert into restraint. Pressure on journalism widened from lawsuits to reported federal investigation. Again and again, courts served as the connective tissue of the week: sometimes checking the administration, sometimes enabling it, and often functioning as the last forum where records, rights, and institutional limits could still be contested.
